entries.13bc84e1a6c6a345ae1188baf547e31b15d48861: <div sID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="143" osisID="Ps.143" sID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> This psalm, as those before, is a prayer of David, and full of complaints of the great distress and danger he was in, probably when Saul persecuted him. He did not only pray in that affliction, but he prayed very much and very often, not the same over again, but new thoughts. In this psalm, I. He complains of his troubles, through the oppression of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">ver. 3</reference>) and the weakness of his spirit under it, which was ready to sink notwithstanding the likely course he took to support himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4-Ps.143.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. II. He prays, and prays earnestly (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">ver. 6</reference>), 1. That God would hear him, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. 2. That he would not deal with him according to his sins, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">ver. 2</reference>. 3. That he would not hide his face from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.7">ver. 7</reference>), but manifest his favour to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">ver. 8</reference>. 4. That he would guide and direct him in the way of his duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">ver. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">10</reference>) and quicken him in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">ver. 11</reference>. 5. That he would deliver him out of his troubles, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">ver. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">11</reference>. 6. That he would in due time reckon with his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.12">ver. 12</reference>. We may more easily accommodate this psalm to ourselves, in the singing of it, because most of the petitions in it are for spiritual blessings (which we all need at all times), mercy and grace.
entries.b963bd8f2c37e65057be5c64e5cadf39cbe3dbc9: <div eID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen13197" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear my prayer, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> in thy righteousness. <hi type="super">2</hi> And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath smitten my life down to the ground; he hath made me to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead. <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore is my spirit overwhelmed within me; my heart within me is desolate. <hi type="super">5</hi> I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works; I muse on the work of thy hands. <hi type="super">6</hi> I stretch forth my hands unto thee: my soul <hi type="italic">thirsteth</hi> after thee, as a thirsty land. Selah. <div eID="gen13197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13198" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David humbly begs to be heard (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">v. 1</reference>), not as if he questioned it, but he earnestly desired it, and was in care about it, for, having desired it, and was in care about it, for having directed his prayer, he looked up to see how it sped, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>. He is a suppliant to his God, and he begs that his requests may be granted: <hi type="italic">Hear my prayer; give ear to my supplications.</hi> He is an appellant against his persecutors, and he begs that his case may be brought to hearing and that God will give judgment upon it, in his faithfulness and righteousness, as the Judge of right and wrong. Or, "Answer my petitions in thy faithfulness, according to the promises thou hast made, which thou wilt be just to." We have no righteousness of our own to plead, and therefore must plead God's righteousness, the word of promise which he has freely given us and caused us to hope in. <div eID="gen13198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13199" type="x-p"/> II. He humbly begs not to be proceeded against in strict justice, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">v. 2</reference>. He seems here, if not to correct, yet to explain, his plea (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">v. 1</reference>), Deliver me <hi type="italic">in thy righteousness;</hi> "I mean," says he, "the righteous promises of the gospel, not the righteous threatenings of the law; if I be answered according to the righteousness of this broken covenant of innocency, I am quite undone;" and therefore, 1. His petition is, "<hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with thy servant;</hi> do not deal with me in strict justice, as I deserve to be dealt with." In this prayer we must own ourselves to be God's servants, bound to obey him, accountable to him, and solicitous to obtain his favour, and we must approve ourselves to him. We must acknowledge that in many instances we have offended him, and have come short of our duty to him, that he might justly enquire into our offences, and proceed against us for them according to law, and that, if he should do so, judgment would certainly go against us; we have nothing to move in arrest or mitigation of it, but execution would be taken out and awarded and then we should be ruined for ever. But we must encourage ourselves with a hope that there is mercy and forgiveness with God, and be earnest with him for the benefit of that mercy. "<hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with thy servant,</hi> for thou hast already entered into judgment with thy Son, and laid upon him the iniquity of us all. <hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with thy servant,</hi> for thy servant enters into judgment with himself;" and, if <hi type="italic">we will judge ourselves, we shall not be judged.</hi> 2. His plea is, "<hi type="italic">In thy sight shall no man living be justified</hi> upon those terms, for no man can plead innocency nor any righteousness of his own, either that he has not sinned or that he does not deserve to die for his sins; nor that he has any satisfaction of his own to offer;" nay, if God contend with us, <hi type="italic">we are not able to answer him for one of a thousand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.3">Job ix. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">xv. 20</reference>. David, before he prays for the removal of his trouble, prays for the pardon of his sin, and depends upon mere mercy for it. <div eID="gen13199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13200" type="x-p"/> III. He complains of the prevalency of his enemies against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">v. 3</reference>): "Saul, that great enemy, <hi type="italic">has persecuted my soul,</hi> sought my life, with a restless malice, and has carried the persecution so far that he has already <hi type="italic">smitten it down to the ground.</hi> Though I am not yet under ground, I am struck to the ground, and that is next door to it; he has forced me to <hi type="italic">dwell in darkness,</hi> not only in dark caves, but in dark thoughts and apprehensions, in the clouds of melancholy, <hi type="italic">as</hi> helpless and hopeless as <hi type="italic">those that have been long dead.</hi> Lord, let me find mercy with thee, for I find no mercy with men. They condemn me; but, Lord, do not thou condemn me. Am not I an object of thy compassion, fit to be appeared for; and is not my enemy an object of thy displeasure, fit to be appeared against?" <div eID="gen13200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> IV. He bemoans the oppression of his mind, occasioned by his outward troubles (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore is my spirit</hi> overpowered and <hi type="italic">overwhelmed within me,</hi> and I am almost plunged in despair; when without are fightings within are fears, and those fears greater tyrants and oppressors than Saul himself and not so easily out-run. It is sometimes the lot of the best men to have their spirits for a time almost overwhelmed and their hearts desolate, and doubtless it is their infirmity. David was not only a great saint, but a great soldier, and yet even he was sometimes ready to faint in a day of adversity. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be shaken.</hi> <div eID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> V. He applies himself to the use of proper means for the relief of his troubled spirit. He had no force to muster up against the oppression of the enemy, but, if he can keep possession of nothing else, he will do what he can to keep possession of his own soul and to preserve his inward peace. In order to this, 1. He looks back, and <hi type="italic">remembers the days of old</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.5">v. 5</reference>), God's former appearances for his afflicted people and for him in particular. It has been often a relief to the people of God in their straits to think of the wonders which their fathers told them of, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.5">Ps. lxxvii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.11">11</reference>. 2. He looks round, and takes notice of the works of God in the visible creation, and the providential government of the world: <hi type="italic">I meditate on all thy works.</hi> Many see them, but do not see the footsteps of God's wisdom, power, and goodness in them, and do not receive the benefit they might by them because they do not meditate upon them; they do not dwell on that copious curious subject, but soon quit it, as if they had exhausted it, when they have scarcely touched upon it. <hi type="italic">I muse on,</hi> or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">I discourse of, the</hi> operation <hi type="italic">of thy hands,</hi> how great, how good, it is! The more we consider the power of God the less we shall fear the face or force of man, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 12, 13</reference>. 3. He looks up with earnest desires towards God and his favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I stretch forth my hands unto thee,</hi> as one begging an alms, and big with expectation to receive something great, standing ready to lay hold on it and bid it welcome. <hi type="italic">My soul thirsteth after thee; it is to thee</hi> (so the word is), entire for thee, intent on thee; it is <hi type="italic">as a thirsty land,</hi> which, being parched with excessive heat, gapes for rain; so do I need, so do I crave, the support and refreshment of divine consolations under my afflictions, and nothing else will relieve me." This is the best course we can take when our spirits are overwhelmed; and justly do those sink under their load who will not take such a ready way as this to ease themselves.
entries.eabfece34f6f6dd7cc1d1e7d8985ae06a48fb9b7: <div eID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayers for Divine Grace.</title> <div sID="gen13203" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hear me speedily, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : my spirit faileth: hide not thy face from me, lest I be like unto them that go down into the pit. <hi type="super">8</hi> Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning; for in thee do I trust: cause me to know the way wherein I should walk; for I lift up my soul unto thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> Deliver me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me. <hi type="super">10</hi> Teach me to do thy will; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my God: thy spirit <hi type="italic">is</hi> good; lead me into the land of uprightness. <hi type="super">11</hi> Quicken me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , for thy name's sake: for thy righteousness' sake bring my soul out of trouble. 12 And of thy mercy cut off mine enemies, and destroy all them that afflict my soul: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy servant. <div eID="gen13203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13204" type="x-p"/> David here tells us what he said when he stretched forth his hands unto God; he begins not only as one in earnest, but as one in haste: "<hi type="italic">Hear me speedily,</hi> and defer no longer, for <hi type="italic">my spirit faileth.</hi> I am just ready to faint; reach the cordial—quickly, quickly, or I am gone." It was not a haste of unbelief, but of vehement desire and holy love. <hi type="italic">Make haste, O God! to help me.</hi> Three things David here prays for:— <div eID="gen13204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13205" type="x-p"/> I. The manifestations of God's favour towards him, that God would be well pleased with him and let him know that he was so; this he prefers before any good, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Ps. iv. 6</reference>. 1. He dreads God's frowns: "Lord, <hi type="italic">hide not thy face from me;</hi> Lord, be not angry with me, do not turn from me, as we do from one we are displeased with; Lord, let me not be left under the apprehensions of thy anger or in doubt concerning thy favour; if I have thy favour, let it not be hidden from me." Those that have the truth of grace cannot but desire the evidence of it. He pleads the wretchedness of his case if God withdrew from him: "Lord, let me not lie under thy wrath, for then I am <hi type="italic">like those that go down to the pit,</hi> that is, down to the grave (I am a dead man, weak, and pale, and ghastly; thy frowns are worse than death), or down to hell, the bottomless pit." Even those who through grace are delivered from going down to the pit may sometimes, when the terrors of the Almighty set themselves in array against them, look like those who are going to the pit. Disconsolate saints have sometimes cried out of the wrath of God, as if they had been damned sinners, <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job vi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.6">Ps. lxxxviii. 6</reference>. 2. He entreats God's favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning.</hi> He cannot but think that God has a kindness for him, that he has some kind things to say to him, some good words and comfortable words; but the present hurry of his affairs, and tumult of his spirits, drowned those pleasing whispers; and therefore he begs, "Lord, do not only speak kindly to me, but cause me to hear it, to <hi type="italic">hear joy and gladness,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.51.8">Ps. li. 8</reference>. God speaks to us by his word and by his providence, and in both we should desire and endeavour to <hi type="italic">hear his lovingkindness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.43">Ps. cvii. 43</reference>), that we may set that always before us: "<hi type="italic">Cause me to hear</hi> it <hi type="italic">in the morning,</hi> every morning; let my waking thoughts be of God's lovingkindness, that the sweet relish of that may abide upon my spirits all the day long." His plea is, "<hi type="italic">For in thee do I trust,</hi> and in thee only; I look not for comfort in any other." God's goodness is commonly wrought <hi type="italic">for those who trust in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Ps. xxxi. 8</reference>), who by faith draw it out. <div eID="gen13205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13206" type="x-p"/> II. The operations of God's grace in him. Those he is as earnest for as for the tokens of God's favour to him, and so should we be. He prays, <div eID="gen13206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13207" type="x-p"/> 1. That he might be enlightened with the knowledge of God's will; and this is the first work of the Spirit, in order to his other works, for God deals with men as men, as reasonable creatures. Here are three petitions to this effect:— (1.) <hi type="italic">Cause me to know the way wherein I should walk.</hi> Sometimes those that are much in care to walk right are in doubt, and in the dark, which is the right way. Let them come boldly to the throne of grace, and beg of God, by his word, and Spirit, and providence, to show them the way, and prevent their missing it. A good man does not ask what is the way in which he must walk, or in which is the most pleasant walking, but what is the right way, the way in which he should walk. He pleads, "<hi type="italic">I lift up my soul unto thee,</hi> to be moulded and fashioned according to thy will." He did not only importunately, but impartially, desire to know his duty; and those that do so shall be taught. (2.) "<hi type="italic">Teach me to do thy will,</hi> not only show me what thy will is, but teach me how to do it, how to turn my hand dexterously to my duty." It is the desire and endeavour of all God's faithful servants to know and to do his will, and to stand complete in it. He pleads, "<hi type="italic">Thou art my God,</hi> and therefore my oracle, by whom I may expect to be advised—my God, and therefore my ruler, whose will I desire to do." If we do in sincerity take God for our God, we may depend upon him to teach us to do his will, as a master does his servant. (3.) <hi type="italic">Lead me into the land of uprightness,</hi> into the communion of saints, that pleasant land of the upright, or into a settled course of holy living, which will lead to heaven, that land of uprightness where holiness will be in perfection, and he that is holy shall be holy still. We should desire to be led, and kept safe, to heaven, not only because it is a land of blessedness, but because it is a land of uprightness; it is the perfection of grace. We cannot find the way that will bring us to that land unless God show us, nor go in that way unless he take us by the hand and lead us, as we lead those that are weak, or lame, or timorous, or dim-sighted; so necessary is the grace of God, not only to put us into the good way, but to keep us and carry us on in it. The plea is, "<hi type="italic">Thy Spirit is good,</hi> and able to make me good," good and willing to help those that are at a loss. Those that have the Lord for their God have his Spirit for their guide; and it is both their character and their privilege that they are <hi type="italic">led by the Spirit.</hi> <div eID="gen13207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13208" type="x-p"/> 2. He prays that he might be enlivened to do his will (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Quicken me, O Lord!</hi>—quicken my devotions, that they may be lively; quicken me to my duty, and quicken me in it; and this <hi type="italic">for thy name's sake.</hi>" The best saints often find themselves dull, and dead, and slow, and therefore pray to God to quicken them. <div eID="gen13208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13209" type="x-p"/> III. The appearance of God's providence for him, 1. That God would, in his own way and time, give him rest from his troubles (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Deliver me, O Lord! from my enemies,</hi> that they may not have their will against me; <hi type="italic">for I flee unto thee to hide me;</hi> I trust to thee to defend me in my trouble, and therefore to rescue me out of it." Preservations are pledges of salvation, and those shall find God their hiding-place who by faith make him such. He explains himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For thy righteousness-sake, bring my soul out of trouble,</hi> for thy promise-sake, nay, for thy mercy-sake" (for some by <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> understand <hi type="italic">kindness</hi> and <hi type="italic">goodness</hi>); "do not only deliver me from my outward trouble, but from the trouble of my soul, the trouble that threatens to overwhelm my spirit. Whatever trouble I am in, Lord, let not my heart be troubled," <reference osisRef="John.14.1">John xiv. 1</reference>. 2. That he would reckon with those that were the instruments of his trouble (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Of thy mercy</hi> to me <hi type="italic">cut off my enemies,</hi> that I may be no longer in fear of them; <hi type="italic">and destroy all those,</hi> whoever they be, how numerous, how powerful, soever, <hi type="italic">who afflict my soul,</hi> and create vexation to that; <hi type="italic">for I am thy servant,</hi> and am resolved to continue such, and therefore may expect to be owned and protected in thy service." This prayer is a prophecy of the utter destruction of all the impenitent enemies of Jesus Christ and his kingdom, who will not have him to reign over them, who grieve his Spirit, and afflict his soul, by afflicting his people, in whose afflictions he is afflicted.  <chapter eID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen13209" type="x-p"/>

entries.427dc326ec910822ce54113243a99a866cb768bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7103"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 143</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference>. In structure and style, like the preceding (Psalms 104-142), this Psalm is clearly evinced to be David's. It is a prayer for pardon, and for relief from enemies; afflictions, as usual, producing confession and penitence.</title> <div sID="gen10891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7103"/><hi type="bold">1. in thy faithfulness ... and ... righteousness--</hi>or, God's regard to the claims which He has permitted His people to make in His covenant. <div eID="gen10891" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1e6c59bf2d80f95acd22af4b1ad1ad9e377d0a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7104"/><div sID="gen10892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7104"/><hi type="bold">2. enter ... judgment--</hi>deal not in strict justice.<div eID="gen10892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall no ... justified--</hi>or, "is no man justified," or "innocent" (<reference osisRef="Job.14.3">Job 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.20">Ro 3:20</reference>). <div eID="gen10893" type="x-p"/>
entries.88cc1983abab112f5ce5b9e49c5cb54a4d975f60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7105"/><div sID="gen10894" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7105"/><hi type="bold">3-4. The exciting reason for his prayer--</hi>his afflictions--led to confession as just made: he now makes the complaint.<div eID="gen10894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as those that have been long dead--</hi>deprived of life's comforts (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.3-Ps.88.6">88:3-6</reference>). <div eID="gen10895" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fc1ca9acb65d31a842290f5fb4fa950beb464d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7106"/><div sID="gen10896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7106"/>5-6. The distress is aggravated by the contrast of former comfort (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.3-Ps.22.5">Psa 22:3-5</reference>), for whose return he longs.<div eID="gen10896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a thirsty land--</hi>which needs rain, as did his spirit God's gracious visits (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.17">89:17</reference>). <div eID="gen10897" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eb37ebce6ceee72bc69ef9ecddc21df9dea419c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7107"/><div sID="gen10898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7107"/><hi type="bold">7. spirit faileth--</hi>is exhausted. <div eID="gen10898" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0eb88660ef07bcf1ec840bdc407dc47bc8164d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7108"/><div sID="gen10899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7108"/>8. (Compare Psa 25:1-4; 59:16).<div eID="gen10899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way ... walk--</hi>that is, the way of safety and righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.3-Ps.142.6">Psa 142:3-6</reference>). <div eID="gen10900" type="x-p"/>
entries.118a297c98d3da4a1389a7b02b48d0275feb5c44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7109"/><div sID="gen10901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7109"/>9. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.31.15-Ps.31.20">Psa 31:15-20</reference>). <div eID="gen10901" type="x-p"/>
entries.64ee3ac08bd3bba7f1b761b8c43e624fdb656844: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7110"/><div sID="gen10902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7110"/>10. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">27:11</reference>).<div eID="gen10902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land of uprightness--</hi>literally, "an even land" (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.12">Psa 26:12</reference>). <div eID="gen10903" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf84c3fe9f251634670eff134034ea10fd9c0ec1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7111"/><div sID="gen10904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7111"/>11. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Psa 23:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.156">119:156</reference>). <div eID="gen10904" type="x-p"/>
entries.49f809959b0cf2777b3afc3ac7b482b2c46b4a67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7112"/><div sID="gen10905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7112"/>12. God's mercy to His people is often wrath to His and their enemies (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.31.17">Psa 31:17</reference>).<div eID="gen10905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy servant--</hi>as chosen to be such, entitled to divine regard. <chapter eID="Ps.143"/>

entries.0bbadbd82909be9fe9cd588ad7e1743486e81941: <div eID="gen23420" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23421" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23422" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23422" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23421" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23423" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays for mercy, and deprecates judgment, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.1">Psa 143:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.2">Psa 143:2</reference>. His persecutions, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.3">Psa 143:3</reference>. His earnest prayer for deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.4-Psa.143.9">Psa 143:4-9</reference>. Prays for God's quickening Spirit, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.10">Psa 143:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.11">Psa 143:11</reference>. And for the total discomfiture of his adversaries, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.12">Psa 143:12</reference> <div eID="gen23423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23424" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew and all the Versions attribute this Psalm to David; and the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Arabic state that it was composed on the rebellion of his son Absalom: nor is there any thing in the Psalm that positively disagrees with this inscription. This is the last of the seven Psalms styled penitential. <div eID="gen23424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23425" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23426" type="x-p"/> In thy faithfulness answer me - Thou hast promised to support me in my difficulties, and, though my children should forsake me, never to withdraw thy loving-kindness from me. See the present unnatural rebellion of my son. Lord, undertake for me!
entries.cbbe5bd8271d43923d67640d1cd5faf3eae201f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23427" type="x-p"/> Enter not into judgment - אל תבוא al tabo. Do not come into court, either as a Witness against me, or as a Judge, else I am ruined; for thou hast seen all my ways that they are evil, and thy justice requires thee to punish me. Nor can any soul that has ever lived be justified in the sight of thy justice and righteousness. Had I my desert from thee, I should have worse than even my unnatural son intends me. O what a relief is Jesus crucified to a soul in such circumstances!
entries.1864e7731dc451289772df4bc2666a67bee936ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23428" type="x-p"/> He hath made me to dwell in darkness - Literally, in dark places. This may be understood of David's taking refuge in caves and dens of the earth, to escape from his persecuting son; yea, even to take refuge in the tombs, or repositories of the dead.
entries.180ae318e7e6fad78acd3e24135361af9c184bac: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23429" type="x-p"/> Therefore is my spirit - I am deeply depressed in spirit, and greatly afflicted in body. <div eID="gen23429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23430" type="x-p"/> My heart within me is desolate - It has no companion of its sorrows, no sympathetic friend. I am utterly destitute of comfort.
entries.007342f9e424f684d9c993e92d1b520f6f13068c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23431" type="x-p"/> I remember the days of old - Thou hast often helped me, often delivered me. I will therefore trust in thee, for thy mercy is not clean gone from me.
entries.b7183a213fa921aedcdfa82435e47edee4e27eb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23432" type="x-p"/> I stretch forth my hands - This is a natural action. All in distress, or under the influence of eager desire, naturally extend their hands and arms, as if to catch at help and obtain succor. <div eID="gen23432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23433" type="x-p"/> As a thirsty land - Parched and burned by the sun, longs for rain, so does my thirsty soul for the living God.
entries.0ee8024c0cd45b1a7414b08b3962e932429e7944: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23434" type="x-p"/> Hear me speedily - מהר maher, make haste to answer me. A few hours, and my state may be irretrievable. In a short time my unnatural son may put an end to my life.
entries.f02d8dbbd1be031fecefd24151fd3059c261da22: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23435" type="x-p"/> Cause me to hear thy Loving-kindness in the morning - This petition was probably offered in the night-season. David had despatched his messengers in all directions; and prays to God that he might by the morning get some good news. <div eID="gen23435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23436" type="x-p"/> Cause me to know the way wherein I should walk - Absalom and his partisans are in possession of all the country. I know not in what direction to go, that I may not fall in with them: point out by thy especial providence the path I should take.
entries.4a347e5a579a342e7968cc09f1491dfc1c64ecae: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23437" type="x-p"/> I flee unto thee to hide me - That I may not be found by my enemies, who seek my life to destroy it.
entries.61ea1ecbc791ed072d2c0bc01bdf6560ca496ac1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23438" type="x-p"/> Teach me to do thy will - רצונך retsonecha, thy pleasure. To be found doing the will of God is the only safe state for man. <div eID="gen23438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23439" type="x-p"/> Thy Spirit is good - The Author of every good desire and holy purpose. <div eID="gen23439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23440" type="x-p"/> Lead me - Let it lead me by its continued inspirations and counsels. <div eID="gen23440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23441" type="x-p"/> Into the land of uprightness - "Into a right land," Chaldee. Into the place where I shall be safe. The old Psalter has, Thi goste gude sal lede me into rygt lande.
entries.a317dc9c75fd0afa5ccf36fc5a87a8461f829983: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23442" type="x-p"/> Quicken me - I am as a dead man, and my hopes are almost dead within me.
entries.3cb40423905dcc32d6f6e5fc22d839bbd621440c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23443" type="x-p"/> And of thy mercy - To me and the kingdom. <div eID="gen23443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23444" type="x-p"/> Cut off mine enemies - Who, if they succeed, will destroy the very form of godliness. The steps he has already taken show that even morality shall have no countenance, if Absalom reign. <div eID="gen23444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23445" type="x-p"/> I am thy servant - Whoever is disloyal to me, I will love and serve thee. <div eID="gen23445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23446" type="x-p"/> For a full explanation of this Psalm, as applied to penitents, see the analysis.  <chapter eID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen23446" type="x-p"/>

entries.909421b3af6556d2fd7f7103eaa6e6011abbd5c3: <div eID="gen10308" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Longing after Mercy in the Midst of Dark Imprisonment</title> <div sID="gen10309" type="x-p"/> In some codices of the lxx this Psalm (as Euthymius also bears witness) has no inscription at all; in others, however, it has the inscription: Ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαυεὶδ ὅτε αὐτὸν ἐδίωκεν Ἀβεσσαλὼμ ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ (<hi type="italic">Cod. Sinait.</hi> οτε αυτον ο υς καταδιωκει). Perhaps by the same poet as <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>, with which it accords in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">Psa 143:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">Psa 143:11</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>, 8), it is like this a modern offshoot of the Davidic Psalm-poetry, and is certainly composed as coming out of the situation of him who was persecuted by Absalom. The Psalms of this time of persecution are distinguished from those of the time of the persecution by Saul by the deep melancholy into which the mourning of the dethroned king was turned by blending with the penitential sorrowfulness of one conscious of his own guilt. On account of this fundamental feature the church has chosen <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference> for the last of its seven <hi type="italic">Psalmi poenitentiales</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Sela</hi> at the close of <reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">Psa 143:6</reference> divides the Psalm into two halves.
entries.2af36844914e04431ee859dbbcc15ad193eeda2b: <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.6">Psa 143:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen10309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10310" type="x-p"/> The poet pleads two motives for the answering of his prayer which are to be found in God Himself, viz., God’s אמוּנה, truthfulness, with which He verifies the truth of His promises, that is to say, His faithfulness to His promises; and His צדקה, righteousness, not in a recompensative legal sense, but in an evangelical sense, in accordance with His counsel, i.e., the strictness and earnestness with which He maintains the order of salvation established by His holy love, both against the ungratefully disobedient and against those who insolently despise Him. Having entered into this order of salvation, and within the sphere of it serving Jahve as his God and Lord, the poet is the servant of Jahve. And because the conduct of the God of salvation, ruled by this order of salvation, or His “righteousness” according to its fundamental manifestation, consists in His justifying the sinful man who has no righteousness that he can show corresponding to the divine holiness, but penitently confesses this disorganized relationship, and, eager for salvation, longs for it to be set right again - because of all this, the poet prays that He would not also enter into judgment (בּוא בּמשׁפּט as in <reference osisRef="Job.9.32">Job 9:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.4">Job 22:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.3">Job 14:3</reference>) with him, that He therefore would let mercy instead of justice have its course with him. For, apart from the fact that even the holiness of the good spirits does not coincide with God’s absolute holiness, and that this defect must still be very far greater in the case of spirit-corporeal man, who has earthiness as the basis of his origin-yea, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.51.7">Psa 51:7</reference>, man is conceived in sin, so that he is sinful from the point at which he begins to live onward - his life is indissolubly interwoven with sin, no living man possesses a righteousness that avails before God (<reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.2">Job 9:2</reference>; Job 14:3., <reference osisRef="Job.15.14">Job 15:14</reference>, and frequently).<note placement="foot">Gerson observes on this point (vid., Thomasius, <hi type="italic">Dogmatik</hi>, iv. 251): I desire the righteousness of pity, which Thou bestowest in the present life, not the judgment of that righteousness which Thou wilt put into operation in the future life - the righteousness which justifies the repentant one.</note> <div eID="gen10310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10311" type="x-p"/> With כּי (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">Psa 143:3</reference>) the poet introduces the ground of his petition for an answer, and more particularly for the forgiveness of his guilt. He is persecuted by deadly foes and is already nigh unto death, and that not without transgression of his own, so that consequently his deliverance depends upon the forgiveness of his sins, and will coincide with this. “The enemy persecuteth my soul” is a variation of language taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference> (חיּה for חיּים, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.50">Psa 78:50</reference>, and frequently in the Book of Job, more particularly in the speeches of Elihu). <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">Psa 143:3</reference></hi> also recalls <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference>, but as to the words it sounds like <reference osisRef="Lam.3.6">Lam 3:6</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.88.7">Psa 88:7</reference>). מתי עולם (lxx νεκροὺς αἰῶνος) are either those for ever dead (the Syriac), after שׁנת עולם in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jer 51:39</reference>, cf. בּית עולמו in <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.5">Ecc 12:5</reference>, or those dead time out of mind (Jerome), after עם עולם in Eze 26:20. The genitive construction admits both senses; the former, however, is rendered more natural by the consideration that הושׁיבני glances back to the beginning that seems to have no end: the poet seems to himself like one who is buried alive for ever. In consequence of this hostility which aims at his destruction, the poet feels his spirit within him, and consequently his inmost life, veil itself (the expression is the same as <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference>); and in his inward part his heart falls into a state of disturbance (ישׁתּומם, a <hi type="italic">Hithpo</hi>. peculiar to the later language), so that it almost ceases to beat. He calls to mind the former days, in which Jahve was manifestly with him; he reflects upon the great redemptive work of God, with all the deeds of might and mercy in which it has hitherto been unfolded; he meditates upon the doing (בּמעשׂה, Ben-Naphtali בּמעשׂה) of His hands, i.e., the hitherto so wondrously moulded history of himself and of his people. They are echoes out of <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4-Ps.77.7">Psa 77:4-7</reference>, Psa 77:12. The contrast which presents itself to the Psalmist in connection with this comparison of his present circumsntaces with the past opens his wounds still deeper, and makes his prayer for help all the more urgent. He stretches forth his hands to God that He may protect and assist him (vid., Hölemann, <hi type="italic">Bibelstudien</hi>, i. 150f.). Like parched land is his soul turned towards Him, - language in which we recognise a bending round of the primary passage Psa 63:2. Instead of לך it would be לך, if סלה (Targum לעלמין) were not, as it always is, taken up and included in the sequence of the accents.
entries.e070b69293a7e34fbe3bbe69986ffd71324bdd1b: <reference osisRef="Ps.143.7-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:7-12</reference> <div eID="gen10311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10312" type="x-p"/> In this second half the Psalm seems still more like a reproduction of the thoughts of earlier Psalms. The prayer, “answer me speedily, hide not Thy face from me,” sounds like <reference osisRef="Ps.69.18">Psa 69:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">Psa 27:9</reference>, cf. Psa 102:3. The expression of languishing longing, כּלתה רוּחי, is like Psa 84:3. And the apodosis, “else I should become like those who go down into the pit,” agrees word for word with <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>, cf. Psa 88:5. In connection with the words, “cause me to hear Thy loving-kindness in the early morning,” one is reminded of the similar prayer of Moses in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference>, and with the confirmatory “for in Thee do I trust” of <reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference>, and frequently. With the prayer that the night of affliction may have an end with the next morning’s dawn, and that God’s helping loving-kindness may make itself felt by him, is joined the prayer that God would be pleased to grant him to know the way that he has to go in order to escape the destruction into which they are anxious to ensnare him. This last prayer has its type in <reference osisRef="Exod.33.13">Exo 33:13</reference>, and in the Psalter in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.4">Psa 25:4</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>); and its confirmation: for to Thee have I lifted up my soul, viz., in a craving after salvation and in the confidence of faith, has its type in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>; Psa 86:4. But the words אליך כסּיתי, which are added to the petition “deliver me from mine enemies” (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.2">Psa 59:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">Psa 31:16</reference>), are peculiar, and in their expression without example. The Syriac version leaves them untranslated. The lxx renders: ὅτι πρὸς σὲ κατέφυγον, by which the defective mode of writing כסתי is indirectly attested, instead of which the translators read נסתי (cf. נוּס על in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa 10:3</reference>); for elsewhere not חסה but נוּס is reproduced with καταφυγεῖν. The Targum renders it מימרך מנּתי לפריק, Thy Logos do I account as (my) Redeemer (i.e., regard it as such), as if the Hebrew words were to be rendered: upon Thee do I reckon or count, כסּיתי = כּסתּי, Exo 12:4. Luther closely follows the lxx: “to Thee have I fled for refuge.” Jerome, however, inasmuch as he renders: <hi type="italic">ad te protectus sum</hi>, has pointed כסּיתי (כסּיתי). Hitzig (on the passage before us and <reference osisRef="Prov.7.20">Pro 7:20</reference>) reads כסתי from כּסא = סכא, to look (“towards Thee do I look”). But the Hebrew contains no trace of that verb; the full moon is called כסא (כסה), not as being “a sight or vision, <hi type="italic">species</hi>,” but from its covered orb. <div eID="gen10312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10313" type="x-p"/> The כסּתי before us only admits of two interpretations: (1) <hi type="italic">Ad</hi> (<hi type="italic">apud</hi>) <hi type="italic">te texi</hi> = to Thee have I secretly confided it (Rashi, Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Coccejus, J. H. Michaelis, J. D. Michalis, Rosenmüller, Gesenius, and De Wette). But such a <hi type="italic">constructio praegnans</hi>, in connection with which כּסּה would veer round from the signification to veil (cf. כסה מן, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Gen 18:17</reference>) into its opposite, and the clause have the meaning of כּי אליך גּלּיתי, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.20">Jer 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.12">Jer 20:12</reference>, is hardly conceivable. (2) <hi type="italic">Ad</hi> (<hi type="italic">apud</hi>) <hi type="italic">te abscondidi</hi>, scil. <hi type="italic">me</hi> (Saadia, Calvin, Maurer, Ewald, and Hengstenberg), in favour of which we decide; for it is evident from <reference osisRef="Gen.38.14">Gen 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.22.12">Deu 22:12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.6">Jon 3:6</reference>, that כּסּה can express the act of covering as an act that is referred to the person himself who covers, and so can obtain a reflexive meaning. Therefore: towards Thee, with Thee have I made a hiding = hidden myself, which according to the sense is equivalent to חסיתּי, as Hupfeld (with a few MSS) wishes to read; but Abulwalîd has already remarked that the same goal is reached with כסּתי. Jahve, with whom he hides himself, is alone able to make known to him what is right and beneficial in the position in which he finds himself, in which he is exposed to temporal and spiritual dangers, and is able to teach him to carry out the recognised will of God (“the will of God, good and well-pleasing and perfect,” <reference osisRef="Rom.12.2">Rom 12:2</reference>); and this it is for which he prays to Him in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">Psa 143:10</reference> (רצונך; another reading, רצונך). For Jahve is indeed his God, who cannot leave him, who is assailed and tempted without and within, in error; may His good Spirit then (רוּחך טובה for הטּובה, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">Neh 9:20</reference>)<note placement="foot">Properly, “Thy Spirit, רוּח הטּובה, a spirit, the good one, although such irregularities may also be a negligent usage of the language, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">msjd 'l - jâm‛</hi>, the chief mosque, which many grammarians regard as a construct relationship, others as an ellipsis (inasmuch as they supply Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - mkân</hi> between the words); the former is confirmed from the Hebrew, vid., Ewald, §287, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.)</note> lead him in a level country, for, as it is said in Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.7">Isa 26:7</reference>, in looking up to Jahve, “the path which the righteous man takes is smoothness; Thou makest the course of the righteous smooth.” The geographical term ארץ מישׁור, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.21">Jer 48:21</reference>, is here applied spiritually. Here, too, reminiscences of Psalms already read meet us everywhere: cf. on “to do Thy will,” <reference osisRef="Ps.40.9">Psa 40:9</reference>; on “for Thou art my God,” <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>, and frequently; on “Thy good Spirit,” <reference osisRef="Ps.51.14">Psa 51:14</reference>; on “a level country,” and the whole petition, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference> (where the expression is “a level path”), together with <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>; Psa 25:4., Psa 31:4. And the Psalm also further unrolls itself in such now well-known thoughts of the Psalms: For Thy Name’s sake, Jahve (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">Psa 25:11</reference>), quicken me again (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference>, and frequently); by virtue of Thy righteousness be pleased to bring my soul out of distress (Ps 142:8; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">Psa 25:17</reference>, and frequently); and by virtue of Thy loving-kindness cut off mine enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">Psa 54:7</reference>). As in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">Psa 143:1</reference> faithfulness and righteousness, here loving-kindness (mercy) and righteousness, are coupled together; and that so that mercy is not named beside towtsiy', nor righteousness beside תּצמית, but the reverse (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">Psa 143:1</reference>). It is impossible that God should suffer him who has hidden himself in Him to die and perish, and should suffer his enemies on the other hand to triumph. Therefore the poet confirms the prayer for the cutting off (הצמית as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.23">Psa 94:23</reference>) of his enemies and the destruction (האביד, elsewhere אבּד) of the oppressors of his soul (elsewhere צררי) with the words: <hi type="italic">for I am Thy servant</hi>.  <chapter eID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen10313" type="x-p"/>

entries.e8233ae450107a324fbd41c0d43b660b6563680d:
PSALM 143
Although the enemies with whom David had to contend were wicked, and their persecution as unjust as it was cruel, David recognized the just judgment of God in it all, and seeks to conciliate his favor by humbly supplicating pardon. Having complained of the cruelty of his enemies, and declared that amidst all his affliction he still remembered God, he prays for restoration, and the guidance of God’s Spirit, that the remainder of his life might be devoted to his fear.
A Psalm of David.
To the title “A Psalm of David,” some copies of the Septuagint and the Vulgate add — “when his son Absalom pursued him,” (see 2 Samuel 17:24, 25;) and interpreters in general agree that this is the most probable occasion on which it was penned.
Psalm 143:1-3
1. Hear my prayer, O Jehovah! give ear to my supplication, in thy truth answer me, in thy righteousness. 2. And enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. 3. For the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath prostrated my life on the ground: he hath set me in dark places, as the dead of an age.
 
1. Hear my prayer, O Jehovah! It is evident that the oppression of his enemies must have been extreme, when David laments his case in such earnest and pathetic terms. The introductory words show that the grief he felt was great. His reason for speaking of the justice and faithfulness of God in connection we have shown elsewhere. Under the term justice, or righteousness, we are not to suppose that he speaks of merit, or hire, as some ignorantly imagine, but of that goodness of God which leads him to defend his people. To the same effect does he speak of God’s truth or faithfulness; for the best proof he can give of his faithfulness is in not forsaking those whom he has promised to help. In helping his people he shows himself to be a just and true God, both in not frustrating their expectation, and in so far as he shows in this extension of mercy what his nature is, that David very properly encourages himself in prayer by making mention of both.

entries.5c27eb2df5ac66d02e61228d89010654ae1dd128:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="143" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXLIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A Psalm of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm is much of the same nature with the form<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, and seems to have been composed much about the same time and upon the like occasion. This is the last of those which are called Penitential Psalms, the former being <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 6. & 32. & 38. & 51. & 102. & 130.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 HEar my prayer, O LORD, give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> in thy righteousness <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Whereby thou art inclined and engaged to favour righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teous persons and just causes.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> but.</ns0:note> And enter not into judgment with thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But when I appeal to thy righteousness, I do it onely with respect to mine enemies, whose cause as well as their persons is worse than mine, but not in reference to thee, as if I could absolutely justifie my self upon a severe tryal at the Tribunal of thy Justice; for if thou shouldest rigorously exa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mine all the passages of mine heart and life, I dread the thoughts and consequences of it.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 34. 7. Job 4. 17. Rom. 3. 20. Gal. 2. 16.</ns0:note> in thy sight shall no man living be justified <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, upon terms of strict justice, without thy indulgence and infinite mercy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 For <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This is not a reason of what he last said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. but an argument to enforce his petition delivered <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. and repeat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7, &c. For though I am not faultless, if thou shouldest make an exact search into me, yet mine enemies are more culpable and highly unjust, and therefore I hope for thy help against them from thy justice as well as mercy.</ns0:note> the enemy hath persecuted my soul <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> My life; for nothing less will satisfie him.</ns0:note>, he hath smitten my life down to the ground <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He hath beaten me down to the ground where I lie strugling for life.</ns0:note>: he hath made me to dwell in darkness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He hath forced me to have mine abode in dark vaults and caves.</ns0:note>, as those that have been long dead <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Where I am out of sight and memory, and in as <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>orlorn and hopeless a condition in the eye of man, as those that have <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ain long rotting in the grave.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Therefore is my spirit overwhelmed within me <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">See on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 61. 2. & 14<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 3.</ns0:note>: my heart within me is desolate <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Deprived of all hope and comfort. Or, <ns0:hi>is astonished.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 I <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 77. 5. 11.</ns0:note> remember the days of old <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> What thou hast done for thy servants in former times. Which he mentions either, 1. as matter of terror, to consider how unlike God now was to himself and to his former dealings: or, 2. as matter of support from former experience, because God was still the same. Either way it drive him to his prayers, which here follow.</ns0:note>, I meditate on all thy works: I muse on the works of thy hands.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 I stretch forth my hands unto thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">I pray to thee <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ervently. See on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 141. 2.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 63. 1.</ns0:note> my soul <ns0:hi>thirsteth</ns0:hi> after thee <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">After thy favour and help.</ns0:note>, as a thirsty land <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To wit, thirs<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eth for rain.</ns0:note>. Selah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Hear me speedily, O LORD, my spirit faileth: hide not thy face from me <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 28. 1.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>for I am become like,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> lest I be like unto them that go down into the pit <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That are dead and buried, of whom there is no hope.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Cause me to hear thy loving kindness in the morning <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Early, as this phrase is taken, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 90. 14. and else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where, seasonably and speedily.</ns0:note>, for in thee do I trust: cause me to know the way wherein I should walk <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">So as to please thee, and to secure my self.</ns0:note>, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 25. 1.</ns0:note> I lift up my soul unto thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Deliver me, O LORD, from mine enemies: I <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> with thee.</ns0:note> flee unto thee to hide me <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Without whose care these caves and rocks can give me no protection.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 25. 4, 5. & 139. 24.</ns0:note> Teach me to do thy will <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To continue in faithful obedience to thee, notwithstand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing all temp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ations to the contrary.</ns0:note>, for thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> my God: thy spirit <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good, lead me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or rather, as it is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />actly in the Hebrew, and as many both ancient and modern Translators render it, <ns0:hi>Let thy good Spirit lead me.</ns0:hi> Leave me not to my own blind and vain mind or corrupt affections, neither give me up to the evil Spirit, as thou didst <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ut conduct me in all my ways by thy <ns0:hi>good, i. e.</ns0:hi> gracious and holy <ns0:hi>Spirit.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> into the land of uprightness <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in plain</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>even land</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>ground,</ns0:hi> in a straight and smooth path, that I may not stumble nor fall ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther into sin or mischief. This is opposed to the crooked and rugged ways in which sinners are said to walk. See <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 125. 5. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 2. 15. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 40. 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Quicken me, O LORD, for thy Names sake: for thy righteousness sake bring my soul out of trouble.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And of thy mercy <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Out of thy mercy to me, whose life they seek.</ns0:note> cut off mine enemies, and destroy all them that afflict my soul: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 16. 16.</ns0:note> I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> thy servant.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>

Poole.heading: PSAL. CXLIII. A Psalm of David.
